claims.text: Tungsten-based alloys are relevant structural materials for fusion plasma-facing components.
The unperturbed tungsten-alloy baseline contains random or incoherent second phases because nanoprecipitate coherence was not deliberately controlled.
A tailored alloying and heat-treatment protocol can generate stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitates in a tungsten matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces are the structural mediator governing the proposed mechanical improvement.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces reduce interfacial stress concentrations.
Easier dislocation transmission delays dislocation pile-up.
Relieving stress concentrations delays premature crack initiation.
The coherent-precipitate microstructure mitigates premature brittle fracture during high-temperature deformation.
An SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit significantly greater high-temperature plastic strain than an otherwise identical alloy without engineered coherent precipitates.
An SCCP-treated alloy will exhibit greater high-temperature fracture toughness than the control alloy.
Microscopy of the SCCP-treated alloy should show dislocations transmitting across coherent interfaces.
The SCCP-treated alloy should show fewer localized stress concentrations that lead to cracks.
The proposed benefit applies from ambient temperature to approximately 800 °C under conditions relevant to fusion plasma-facing components.
The proposed mechanism generally holds across tungsten-based alloys within the stated temperature range.
The mechanism may not apply to other high-melting-point alloy systems or at temperatures far beyond 800 °C.
The magnitude of ductility or toughness improvement depends on alloy composition, precipitate-size distribution, and processing conditions.
Microcracking may contribute to mechanical behavior in alternative alloy systems.
